subject: Accounting
title: Relevant Costs for Decisions
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Relevant Costs for Decisions.

hook.text: You already spent $50,000 developing a product. Should that affect your decision to launch it?

buildup.text: Sunk costs are money already spent that can't be recovered. They shouldn't influence future decisions.

discovery.text: Relevant costs are future costs that differ between alternatives—only these should guide choices.

twist.text: Human nature clings to sunk costs. The 'we've invested too much to quit' trap destroys value.

climax.text: Smart decision-making ignores the past and focuses on what changes going forward.

punchline.text: Don't let yesterday's spending ruin tomorrow's decision.

quiz.question: What are sunk costs?
options: Past costs that can't be recovered
Future costs that vary by decision

details.summary: Relevant costs are future costs that differ between alternatives being considered. This topic explains how to separate relevant from irrelevant costs, why sunk costs should be ignored, and how to apply this thinking to common business decisions.
details.whyItMatters: Including irrelevant costs—especially sunk costs—in decisions is one of the most common and costly errors in business. Focusing only on relevant costs leads to clearer, more profitable choices.
takeaways: A cost is relevant only if it is a future cost that differs between the alternatives being considered
Sunk costs—already spent and unrecoverable—are never relevant to future decisions
Opportunity costs are always relevant even though they don't appear in accounting records

faq.question: What makes a cost relevant for decision-making?
faq.answer: A relevant cost meets two criteria: it occurs in the future (not already spent) and it differs between the alternatives being evaluated. Past costs and costs that remain the same regardless of the choice are irrelevant to the decision.

faq.question: Why should sunk costs be ignored in decisions?
faq.answer: Sunk costs have already been incurred and cannot be recovered regardless of which alternative is chosen. Including them can lead to the sunk cost fallacy—continuing an unprofitable path just because money was already invested. Only future, avoidable costs matter.
